summary:
Private, adult, consensual conduct between men and between women has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the colonial Penal Code offence at Article 175, which had carried a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment. Enforcement had already stopped: in July 2006 Fiji's High Commissioner in New Zealand confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested.

The enforcement era produced prosecutions. In April 2005 an Australian tourist, Thomas McCosker, and a Fijian man, Dhirendra Nadan, received two-year sentences under Article 175, and the trial judge described the acts as 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Those convictions were overturned in August 2005 by Fiji's highest court as violations of the constitution then in force. Days after the sentences were passed, Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in what he described as the conservative Christian nation.

The 1997 Constitution explicitly prohibited government discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation; Human Rights Watch stated in April 2005 that this made Fiji one of the first two countries worldwide to do so, alongside South Africa. That constitution was abolished in 2009. The Constitution promulgated in September 2013 prohibits unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, sexual orientation, and gender identity and expression under Article 26(3), and in 2013 the government included sexual orientation and gender identity in anti-hate-speech law and in law dealing with discrimination in certain businesses.

The constitutional guarantee has no implementing route for gender markers. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, a gap the Asia Pacific Alliance described in 2023 as producing documented marginalisation and discrimination for trans people despite what it called a constitution unique worldwide in its protection of gender identity and expression. Fiji has no legal gender recognition process. The traditional third-gender population known as vaka sa lewa lewa, assigned male at birth but who dress, act and behave as female, have traditionally been accepted by Fijian society, but that cultural standing carries no legal status.

No relationship recognition is available. The Marriage Act 2002 limits marriage to one man and one woman, Fiji family law provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, and prime ministerial opposition to such recognition was reaffirmed on 26 March 2013, in January 2016 and in 2019.

On care, the Mental Health Decree 2010 provides that persons are not mentally ill if they refuse or fail to express a particular sexual orientation and prohibits conversion therapy by registered mental health professionals, and health professionals are barred from trying to change sexual orientation. Intersex bodily autonomy is unprotected under Fiji law.

On violence, a young transgender woman was brutally murdered in Suva in May 2018. No later anti-trans killing is documented in the sources assembled for this assessment. Reporting of anti-gay violence and hateful discrimination is discouraged by lack of trust in police, attributed to possible harassment, and activist accounts describe physical violence and domestic abuse operating as familial conversion therapy for LGBTQ+ people.

Social climate is shaped by majority Methodist and Catholic denominations and by a Muslim minority of about 6%, which tend to view transgender identities negatively or cross-dressing as sinful behaviour to be corrected. Public displays of affection are not illegal but are generally considered offensive. Reports of societal discrimination and bullying are documented, and social mores regarding sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative with little public support for LGBTQ rights.
tangentialFactors:
The hate-crime killings documented in the sources are the murder on 1 July 2001 in Suva of Red Cross leader John Maurice Scott and his partner Gregory Scrivener in an apparent homophobic attack with possible political motive, and a gay student found dead in Nasinu in September 2017. Neither is recorded as trans-specific, and no trans killing later than May 2018 appears in the sources.

Political contestation over trans participation is on the record. In 2022 the National Federation Party endorsed Divina Loloma, a transgender woman, as the first openly LGBTQ candidate ever endorsed by a political party, while All People's Party leader Tuiloma Tawaivuna criticised the nomination, claiming transgender people are an 'abomination' and 'Biblically wrong'.

Public organising has moved in both directions. The government has in the past cancelled gay pride marches; activists organised IDAHOTB activities on 17 May 2013 and held an IDAHOTB event in Suva in 2017 attended by activists and religious figures; Fiji's first pride parade took place on 17 May 2018 in Lautoka, with a local police escort and an address by former President Epeli Nailatikau.

Comparative framing in the sources runs ahead of implementation. Human Rights Watch placed Fiji alongside South Africa in April 2005 as one of the first two countries to constitutionally bar sexual-orientation discrimination, and the Asia Pacific Alliance described the 2013 gender identity and expression protection as unique worldwide, while recording that no legislation or policy gives it effect for gender markers.
localsOnly:
Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been banned since the Employment Relations Promulgation 2007.

In April 2017 the Ministry of Health confirmed that gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood, after a gay man was refused for his sexual orientation.

Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that LGBTQ organisations cannot register in Fiji.

Residents have no route to change a gender marker and no legal recognition of traditional third-gender identities, which the Asia Pacific Alliance linked in 2023 to documented marginalisation and discrimination.

LGBTQ people and couples face disincentives when reporting anti-gay violence or hateful discrimination, on account of lack of trust in police attributed to possible harassment.
outOfScopeNotes:
Outright International's overview carries an at-a-glance flag stating that same-sex relations are illegal, which contradicts the same overview's statement that same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2010 under the Crimes Act. The conflict is unresolved in the sources.

The GlobalGayz country page is undated and its claim that SOGI discrimination was not banned predates the 2013 Constitution; it is treated as a legacy-era source rather than current law.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa rules, passport or marker requirements, airport screening, or facility access as they apply to trans travellers. Nothing on those subjects should be inferred from this assessment.

No denominator, rate or period count for anti-trans violence is available, and the outcome of the investigation into the May 2018 killing in Suva is not sourced.

Whether Article 26(3) has been applied by any court to a trans petitioner, and the availability or cost of gender-affirming care for visitors, are not sourced.
